# Legacy Sunset & Migration Program — Second Consultation Draft

*How this document is meant to be read.* This is a revision, and it exists because colleagues were generous enough to press hard on the first version. Where the criticism was right — and it mostly was — I have changed the plan rather than defended it. Where I have kept a position, I have tried to say why, and to leave it open for the room to settle.

Two requests before the content. First, the numbers below are **placeholders, deliberately visible so that Finance can correct them** — they are offered as a starting shape, not as positions I hold. Second, I would prefer this circulate to Finance, Legal, Field Leadership and the legacy engineering elders *before* it reaches the leadership meeting, so that by the time it is discussed formally, no one is hearing anything for the first time and no one is put in the position of having to disagree in front of others.

There are now **three gates**. Everything else can proceed quietly in parallel and be adjusted.

---

## 1. What this program is actually about

Not decommissioning. We are transferring a third of our profit from one platform to another *without the customer feeling transferred*, while defusing two slow-burning hazards: unpatched surface area, and institutional memory walking out the door.

Three framing observations carried forward from the first draft, because they survived scrutiny:

- **The announcement is the single largest defection event in the program.** The day we publish a date, procurement at every large account is handed a legitimate reason to run a competitive evaluation. Sequence matters more than timeline.
- **A published date that slips is worse than a longer date held.** Credibility is the currency we are spending.
- **Tooling retains customers; discounts only renew them.** Fear is the real churn driver, and fear responds to demonstrable safety, not to price.

And one correction I now accept as the most important criticism of the first draft: **the previous version was a strategy memo wearing a program plan's clothes.** It had no money in it. That is fixed below, and the financial work now sits *ahead* of the timeline, not behind it.

---

## 2. The financial spine (new — and now the first gate, not an appendix)

The brief says a third of **profit**. The first draft set a target on **revenue**. Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is the entire problem.

### 2.1 The profit bridge

Illustrative, indexed so the shape is arguable even before Finance supplies real figures. Let legacy annual revenue = **100**.

| | Legacy today | Same customer, migrated, flat revenue |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 100 | 100 |
| Cost of delivery | −15 (frozen, on-prem, no hosting) | −25 (hosting, higher support surface) |
| R&D allocation | −3 (development stopped years ago) | −15 (active roadmap) |
| Migration cost, amortised over 3y | 0 | −8 |
| **Contribution** | **≈82** | **≈52** |

The uncomfortable implication, which I would rather we all look at together now than discover at Gate 2: **at 100% customer retention and flat pricing, we lose roughly a third of the contribution this base produces.** Legacy profit is high precisely because we stopped investing. Migration re-imposes the investment.

Therefore the program's success measure changes:

- **Old target:** ≥90% of legacy revenue retained through EOL.
- **Revised target:** ≥90% of legacy revenue retained **and** ≥80% of legacy contribution held at T0+48, recovering to ≥100% by T0+60 through expansion — which requires **net +12–18% price/scope realisation on migration**, delivered through consolidation and upsell rather than list-price increases.

That last clause is the real design constraint on the incentive schemes in §8. Any incentive that structurally forecloses expansion is, on these numbers, a decision to permanently shrink our profit base.

### 2.2 Perpetual-to-subscription conversion (previously absent, and material)

If the legacy base is perpetual-licence-plus-maintenance and the replacement is subscription, we face a **recognised-revenue cliff and a cash trough that occur even at zero churn**. This is not a churn story; it is an accounting and guidance story.

- Model the transition in ratable terms before any date is published.
- Offer **prepaid multi-year subscription** and, where the customer's own capex cycle demands it, a **term-licence bridge** on the new platform, so the customer's procurement model does not become a migration blocker.
- If we are publicly reporting: this is a guidance event. Legal, Finance and IR must be satisfied *before* T0, and the announcement is better placed on or near a scheduled results cycle than dropped between them.

### 2.3 Three paths, priced against each other (Gate 0 deliverable)

We should not choose the migration path by default. The baseline for comparison is **harvest**, not migrate.

| Path | Description | Illustrative shape |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Migrate & convert** | Program as described here | ~55–70% of one year's legacy revenue in total program spend over 4 years; profit trough T0+15 to T0+27; strongest long-term position |
| **B — Harvest at premium** | No parity rebuild, minimal tooling, stepped maintenance uplift, accept 25–40% attrition, EOL at T0+36 | Highest near-term cash, lowest capability, highest relationship damage. **This is the financial baseline every other path must beat.** |
| **C — Divest / carve-out** | Sell or spin the legacy line to a long-tail maintenance specialist | Removes cost curve, monetises tail, serves the most bespoke customers better than we intend to. Partly *mutually exclusive* with A: funding Tier A customers off the platform destroys the asset |
| **C′ — Third-party maintenance partnership** | Retain ownership and customers; contract a specialist firm for sustaining engineering and security | Solves the retirement constraint without divesting. **Strongly recommended as a component of A regardless of path choice** |

**Owner:** CFO with Corporate Development, supported by the program lead.
**Decision forced at Gate 0 (Month 3), not left to drift.** The first draft raised divestiture twice and then orphaned it; that was a way of avoiding a hard conversation, and I should not have done it.

**Quantified trigger:** if the irreducible bespoke core (from §5 triage) exceeds **25% of legacy revenue and is concentrated in fewer than 12 accounts**, or if parity rebuild cost exceeds **1.5× the NPV of retained contribution**, we open a divestiture process for that segment. We run A and C on a dual track until Gate 0 and we do not spend Tier A migration money before that gate closes.

**Program budget cap:** proposed at ≈65% of one year of legacy revenue over four years, with a 15% contingency reserve released only by the steering group. A cap that no one may quietly exceed is kinder to everyone than a budget that is renegotiated in twelve separate conversations.

---

## 3. Two gating questions that must be answered before any date is published

The first draft presented a timeline as settled while two of its preconditions were still Phase 0 tasks. That was inconsistent, and the criticism is accepted.

### 3.1 Deployment-model compatibility (the omission I am most embarrassed by)

If the legacy product is self-managed and the replacement is SaaS-only, then **architecture, not features, is the blocker** for exactly the accounts most likely to defect: data residency, air-gapped or classified environments, regulated sectors with cloud prohibitions, customers whose own compliance regime forbids multi-tenancy. No amount of parity engineering or dual-run tooling solves this.

**Month 1–3 task, before anything else:** quantify legacy revenue sitting in cloud-prohibited or residency-constrained environments. Then a decision at Gate 0 from three options:

1. Fund a **self-managed / sovereign edition** of the new product (expensive, slow, strategically significant — properly a leadership decision, not a program decision).
2. Offer **single-tenant dedicated hosting** in-region as a narrower answer.
3. Classify these accounts as **structurally non-migratable** and route them to path C or C′, with the relationship handled as a deliberate, respectful handover rather than a failure.

If the answer is (1), the timeline in §7 lengthens and I would rather say so now.

### 3.2 Contract archaeology as a *precondition* to the date

The top 50 legacy contracts must be read before T0, hunting for perpetual grants, evergreen support obligations, uptime/patch commitments, source escrow, public-sector and regulated terms, and notice periods.

- The announced timeline is **explicitly conditional** on this review. If perpetual or evergreen rights exist, T0+48 is legally hollow for those accounts and pretending otherwise invites a dispute that would damage far more than the program.
- Where such rights exist, we prepare a **waiver-for-consideration mechanism**: migration funded, price locked, credits granted, in exchange for a documented release of the perpetual entitlement.
- **Source escrow requires its own decision.** Mass escrow release at EOL is an IP problem and a gift to any third-party maintainer or competitor. Preferred substitute, offered proactively and warmly: a **supported continuity option** — the binary plus a named third-party maintenance provider under licence — which serves the customer's actual need (continuity) better than source they cannot realistically build.
- Some customers' own audit or certification regimes require a vendor-supported platform. For them, EOL date = the date they fail an audit. They need earlier engagement and, in some cases, path C′.

---

## 4. Phase 0 — quiet internal work (Months 0–9)

A distinction the first draft blurred: **internal preparation may take nine months; the window of selective external disclosure may not.** Nine months of internal work is prudent. Nine months of privately telling twenty large customers something the rest of the market does not know is a leak, a fairness problem, and possibly a disclosure problem. Corrected in §11.

**Evidence gathering without touching the platform.** "Freeze and harden" and "ship telemetry" contradicted each other, and many customers would refuse the telemetry build anyway. Revised evidence hierarchy, in order of reliance:

1. **Licence-key / entitlement data** — what was purchased and enabled (available now, no build).
2. **Configuration and schema dumps** collected through routine support channels.
3. **Five years of support tickets**, mined for feature mentions.
4. **Structured interviews** with the top 50 accounts' administrators — not sales conversations, technical ones.
5. **Optional telemetry**, offered as an opt-in diagnostic bundle to willing customers only, never as a forced upgrade.

**On the annual-cycle blind spot** — this criticism changed a decision. A six-month observation window will confidently retire a year-end close, statutory report, annual audit export or seasonal batch job, and break a strategic account in month 20. Therefore:

- Cycle-sensitive subsystems (financial close, statutory/regulatory reporting, archival export, scheduled batch) are **exempt from usage-based retirement**. For these, interview and contract evidence outrank telemetry, and the default is *retain or bridge* until positively disproven.
- We commit to observing **at least one full annual cycle** before any cycle-sensitive capability is placed in the retire bucket, even if that means a subset of triage decisions closes at Gate 2 rather than Gate 1.

**Knowledge capture, treated as urgent rather than important.** Retention agreements with the handful of engineers who genuinely hold the model, structured against *deliverables* — recorded architecture walkthroughs, runbooks, failure catalogues, a named and demonstrably competent successor. Pairing rotation. Contractor bench engaged warm. **Bus factor ≥3 per critical subsystem by T0+12, tracked as a program metric with a target.**

**Freeze and harden.** Encapsulate the stack, modern gateway and WAF in front, narrow the network surface, move authentication to the current identity layer, reduce the patch obligation to the smallest defensible set. This converts an open-ended liability into something close to a fixed-cost appliance.

**Third-party maintenance partner selected and contracted by T0+6.** This is the answer to a contradiction the first draft left standing (see §7).

---

## 5. Feature triage — rebuild versus retire

A rule, so the argument happens once and no one has to lose it repeatedly in public.

Score each legacy-only capability on (a) revenue-weighted adoption, (b) existence of a workflow substitute, (c) strategic coherence with the new product, (d) rebuild cost, (e) **cycle sensitivity** (new).

| Bucket | Criteria | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild native** | >15% of legacy revenue, or ≥3 strategic accounts, and consistent with product direction | First-class implementation: dated, funded, on the roadmap |
| **Rebuild as compatibility layer** | Behaviour-bound rather than value-bound — exact semantics matter (report formats, macro syntax, obscure protocols, batch quirks) | Adapter/shim, explicitly labelled a compatibility surface with its own later sunset. Contain the ugliness |
| **Partner or services** | Genuinely bespoke, one or two accounts, high cost, low fit | Partner/SI delivery, funded custom extension, or licensed module. Candidate for path C |
| **Retire with a landing** | Trivial usage, superior path exists, and **not cycle-sensitive** | Retire — never bare. Documented alternative, hands-on transition session, commercial gesture where appropriate |
| **Archive** *(new)* | Needed only for records retention, not operations | **Read-only archival edition** — see §10 |

Nothing enters "retire" without a named alternative and a named human who has walked a real customer through it.

---

## 6. Parity control regime (new — the largest structural gap in the first draft)

The first draft named parity-list growth as the most likely failure mode and then provided no control for it. That was a real omission.

- **Per-account parity freeze:** the list closes **60 days after that account's assessment**, in writing, signed by both sides. Items raised later are handled through change control, not absorbed silently.
- **Fixed parity engineering budget** = 12% of program spend, plus a 20% reserve released only by the steering group.
- **One-in-one-out:** after freeze, a new parity item is accepted only by displacing one of equal or greater effort, chosen with the customer. This makes the trade-off visible and shared rather than adversarial.
- **Named escalation owner:** Product Lead and Program Lead jointly, single decision, 5-day turnaround.
- **Leading indicator with a threshold:** new parity items opened per account per month. Sustained above 1.5 for two consecutive months triggers an out-of-cyc

# Diversification Strategy — First Consultation Draft

*How this document is meant to be read.* This is a first draft written to be argued with, not approved. The numbers are **placeholders left deliberately visible so Finance and Corp Dev can correct them**; they describe a shape, not a position I'm attached to. Several sections are framed as questions rather than recommendations — not out of vagueness, but because a few of them genuinely cannot be settled from where I sit, and pretending otherwise would waste the room's time.

One process request. I'd rather this circulate to Finance, the flagship's business lead, whoever was closest to the two prior attempts (including the people who have since left, if they'll talk to us), and one or two long-standing customers' technical buyers, **before** it reaches the board. By the time it's discussed formally, nothing in it should be new to anyone in the room, and no one should be put in the position of having to disagree in public.

There are **three real decisions** in what follows. Everything else can proceed quietly in parallel and be adjusted.

---

## 1. What we are actually solving for

The board has named the problem as *concentration risk*. I'd like to gently widen that, because the framing determines which answers are even visible.

Ninety-five percent of revenue in one product is a fact, not yet a risk. It becomes a risk in the presence of a **discontinuity** — technology substitution, a channel or platform shift, buyer consolidation, regulatory change, a well-funded entrant willing to lose money for five years. A mature market growing at under 2% is not, by itself, dangerous. It is *dull*, and dullness is a different problem with different remedies.

So there are two distinct concerns tangled together, and it's worth pulling them apart before spending anything:

| Concern | What it actually is | What answers it |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | One shock removes most of our earnings | Reduce correlation of earnings sources; strengthen contracts, channels, balance sheet |
| **Stagnation** | Earnings are safe but will not grow | New demand — which may or may not mean new products |

These pull in different directions. An adjacency that grows nicely but fails in exactly the same scenario the flagship fails in solves stagnation and *nothing* about fragility. I'd propose we make that explicit and test for it (§5, correlation test), because it's the failure mode nobody catches until the shock arrives.

**Three framing observations I'd offer for the room to accept or reject:**

- **The honest baseline is not diversification. It is harvest-and-return.** A profitable niche leader in a slow market, run for cash and capital return, is a perfectly respectable outcome that beats most diversification attempts on a risk-adjusted basis. Unless "do nothing new, return the cash" is a genuinely available answer at every gate, the process becomes theatre and every proposal passes.
- **Our scarce resource is not cash. It is management attention and internal credibility.** Strong reserves are why the previous two attempts were *possible*; they were not sufficient. Cash lets you buy a bad idea faster.
- **Two failures have created an organisational allergy.** Whatever we do next will be watched by people who expect it to fail, some of whom would prefer to be right. That is a design constraint on governance (§8), not a morale problem to be jollied along.

---

## 2. Gate 0 (Months 0–3): the failure autopsy, and the capability audit

These two pieces of work are cheap, fast, and worth more than any market study we could commission. They are the first gate because everything downstream is shaped by what they find.

### 2.1 The autopsy

"They strayed too far from our capabilities" is the received explanation. It may well be right. I'd like to hold it loosely for a few weeks, because it is also a *comfortable* explanation — it locates the fault in the idea rather than in how we ran it, and it conveniently implies the remedy is simply "stay closer to home."

Method, and it should be done by someone with no stake in the answer:

1. Retrieve the original investment memos and board papers. Extract the **stated assumptions** — market size, time to revenue, who would sell it, what margin was promised.
2. Interview everyone who was materially involved, including the departed. Separately, not in a group.
3. Reconstruct the sequence of the actual failure: what broke first, and what the organisation did in response.
4. Classify against a taxonomy, because the remedies are entirely different:

| Failure mode | Signature | Remedy implied |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrong adjacency** | Genuinely no reusable asset; we were a random entrant | Better selection screen (§5) |
| **No distribution advantage** | Good product, our channel wouldn't or couldn't sell it | Channel test before build; separate go-to-market |
| **Metric transplant** | Judged on flagship margins/payback from year one; starved when it looked worse | Different metrics and funding rules (§8) |
| **Attention starvation** | Sponsor's day job reclaimed them; the venture became a side project | Dedicated leadership, protected time, named substitute |
| **Talent adverse selection** | Staffed with whoever was available, not who was best | Career-safe secondments, deliberate staffing |
| **One big bet** | Fully funded up front, no kill points, sunk-cost escalation | Stage gating (§7) |
| **Integration crush** | Acquisition's operating model dissolved into ours | Ring-fence, explicit integration doctrine |
| **Right idea, wrong decade** | Thesis validated later by someone else | Option retention rather than exit |

I'd expect us to find **two or three of these simultaneously**, with "metric transplant" and "attention starvation" more prominent than the official story allows. If so, the implication is uncomfortable but useful: our selection problem may be smaller than our *operating model* problem, and a better screen alone would not have saved either attempt.

**Deliverable:** a two-page classification, circulated to the people interviewed for correction before it goes anywhere else.

### 2.2 The capability audit — what we own that is actually portable

Every company believes it has transferable capabilities. Most of what gets listed is either not rare, not portable, or already fully monetised. The test I'd propose, applied asset by asset:

For each candidate asset, four questions: **Is it rare? Is it hard to copy? Is it portable outside the flagship's context? Is there value left in it that we are not currently capturing?** An asset must pass all four to count.

Likely candidates for a company in our position, with the honest verdict noted:

| Candidate asset | Usual reality |
|---|---|
| **Access to and trust with a specific buyer** | Often the single most valuable and most under-used asset. Demand-side. Portable across *offerings*, not across *buyers* |
| **Deep domain and regulatory knowledge** | Genuinely rare. Portable only within the domain |
| **Installed-base data / operational telemetry** | Frequently valuable, frequently unexamined, occasionally contractually unusable — check before building a thesis on it |
| **Certifications, approvals, audit history** | Rare, expensive to replicate, a real moat where they apply |
| **Support / field / service infrastructure** | Portable, and often has spare capacity |
| **Brand** | Portable *only within the permission the brand carries*. Test it (§5), don't assume it |
| **Engineering or manufacturing competence** | Usually less rare than we believe |
| **Cash** | Not a capability. Please let's not treat it as one |

**The screen I'd propose, and this is the one substantive rule I'd like to hold firm on:** a candidate adjacency must reuse **at least two** audited assets, and **at least one must be demand-side** — customer access, trust, brand permission, channel. Supply-side reuse alone ("we're good at building this sort of thing") produces competent products that nobody has any particular reason to buy from us. My working suspicion is that this is what happened at least once before.

---

## 3. Where to look: an adjacency map, ordered by distance

Rather than a list of ideas, a map of *territories*, ordered from nearest to furthest. Distance correlates with both risk and diversification value, which is the whole tension.

**Ring 0 — Value capture inside the core.** Pricing architecture, packaging and tiering, attach rates, contract length, churn recovery, price realisation in under-monetised segments. Not diversification at all. But it is typically the cheapest earnings growth available to a mature niche leader, it requires no new capability, and — the point — **it can fund the entire diversification programme without touching reserves.** I'd want this run as a parallel workstream from month one by the flagship's own team, with its incremental contribution explicitly earmarked as the programme's funding source. It also buys political cover: a programme funded from found money is much harder to resent.

**Ring 1 — Attach around the flagship.** Consumables, service contracts, extended support tiers, training and certification, financing, implementation and managed services, compliance-as-a-service. Same buyer, same budget, same sales motion. Low diversification value in the fragility sense (correlated with the core), real value in growth and switching cost. Cheap. Do the good ones regardless of what else we decide.

**Ring 2 — Data and insight products from the installed base.** Benchmarking, industry indices, predictive maintenance, regulatory reporting. Uses an asset only we hold. Margin profile usually excellent. Two hard gates: contractual right to use the data, and whether customers will pay for insight they believe they already own. Requires genuine consent-based commercial design, not a legal loophole.

**Ring 3 — Adjacent steps in the buyer's workflow.** What our customer does immediately before and immediately after they use the flagship, and who they currently buy that from. This is, in my view, **the highest-expected-value territory** and where I'd want the most theses. Same buyer, same trust, same procurement path — but a genuinely new offering, new competitors, and often a new demand driver. The interesting question is never "what could we build?" but "which of our customer's adjacent problems is being served badly by someone who doesn't understand the domain?"

**Ring 4 — Same offering, adjacent buyers.** New verticals, new geographies, new segment tiers (a stripped-down offer for the mid-market we currently ignore; a sovereign or regulated variant). Reuses the product; requires new demand-side assets, which is exactly what we can't transfer. Cheaper than it looks on the supply side, more expensive than it looks on the demand side.

**Ring 5 — Capability transplant.** Our technical competence applied to a different customer base entirely. This is almost certainly the territory of at least one previous failure. Not forbidden — but it should be funded and governed as **venture**, at venture-sized cheques, and never as "an extension of the business."

**Ring 6 — Unrelated diversification.** Buying earnings streams for the sake of decorrelation. The board's instinct will drift here, and I'd rather say plainly now that it's a poor use of an operating company's balance sheet. Shareholders can diversify more cheaply than we can. **If the answer to fragility is financial, the right instruments are capital return, contract structure, insurance and balance-sheet strength — not conglomeration.**

**One structural option worth its own line:** open the installed base as a **platform** — let third parties build, certify and sell into our customers, and take a share plus certification revenue. Minimal capital, uses the installed-base asset directly, and produces a live map of which adjacencies customers actually want. It doubles as the cheapest market-research instrument available to us.

---

## 4. Ring 0 caveat: protecting the core comes first

Before any of this, a commitment I'd like written into the programme charter rather than assumed:

- **The flagship's own investment plan is funded in full, first, at pre-programme levels or better.** The fastest way to endanger the core is to quietly tax it.
- **No more than [10]% of named key flagship personnel** may be reassigned to programme work, with the flagship's business lead holding a veto — not an advisory voice, a veto.
- **No customer becomes an unwilling pilot.** Every pilot is opt-in, with a named relationship owner who can stop it, and a written commitment about what happens if it's cancelled.
- **No cross-subsidy in pricing.** Bundling a venture into flagship contracts to manufacture adoption produces revenue that teaches us nothing and hides failure.
- **A cash floor** below which the programme pauses automatically, set by Finance and stated publicly, so that nobody has to be the person who raises it in a bad quarter.

---

## 5. How to evaluate candidates

A scorecard, so the argument happens once and nobody has to lose it repeatedly in meetings. Weights are placeholders; Finance and the flagship lead should set them.

| Criterion | Weight | What good looks like | Kill threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Demand-side asset reuse** | 25 | Same buyer, our name is an advantage | No demand-side reuse → kill |
| **Supply-side asset reuse** | 15 | Two or more audited assets | Fewer than one → kill |
| **Sales-motion compatibility** | 15 | Existing channel can sell it without changing comp | Needs a wholly new channel → reclassify as venture, re-price |
| **Correlation with core demand** | 15 | Fails in a *different* scenario than the flagship | Perfectly correlated → still fundable as growth, but scores zero

## 1. What we are actually solving for

The board has named the problem as *concentration risk*. I'd like to gently widen that, because the framing determines which answers are even visible.

Ninety-five percent of revenue in one product is a fact, not yet a risk. It becomes a risk in the presence of a **discontinuity** — technology substitution, a channel or platform shift, buyer consolidation, regulatory change, a well-funded entrant willing to lose money for five years. | Concern | What it actually is | What answers it |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | One shock removes most of our earnings | Reduce correlation of earnings sources; strengthen contracts, channels, balance sheet |
| **Stagnation** | Earnings are safe but will not grow | New demand — which may or may not mean new products |

These pull in different directions. An adjacency that grows nicely but fails in exactly the same scenario the flagship fails in solves stagnation and *nothing* about fragility. I'd propose we make that explicit and test for it (§5, correlation test), because it's the failure mode nobody catches until the shock arrives.

These two pieces of work are cheap, fast, and worth more than any market study we could commission. They are the first gate because everything downstream is shaped by what they find.

"They strayed too far from our capabilities" is the received explanation. It may well be right. I'd like to hold it loosely for a few weeks, because it is also a *comfortable* explanation — it locates the fault in the idea rather than in how we ran it, and it conveniently implies the remedy is simply "stay closer to home."

Method, and it should be done by someone with no stake in the answer:

1. Retrieve the original investment memos and board papers. Extract the **stated assumptions** — market size, time to revenue, who would sell it, what margin was promised.
2. Interview everyone who was materially involved, including the departed. Separately, not in a group.
3. Reconstruct the sequence of the actual failure: what broke first, and what the organisation did in response.
4. Classify against a taxonomy, because the remedies are entirely different:

| Failure mode | Signature | Remedy implied |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrong adjacency** | Genuinely no reusable asset; we were a random entrant | Better selection screen (§5) |
| **No distribution advantage** | Good product, our channel wouldn't or couldn't sell it | Channel test before build; separate go-to-market |
| **Metric transplant** | Judged on flagship margins/payback from year one; starved when it looked worse | Different metrics and funding rules (§8) |
| **Attention starvation** | Sponsor's day job reclaimed them; the venture became a side project | Dedicated leadership, protected time, named substitute |

| **Integration crush** | Acquisition's operating model dissolved into ours | Ring-fence, explicit integration doctrine |
| **Right idea, wrong decade** | Thesis validated later by someone else | Option retention rather than exit |

I'd expect us to find **two or three of these simultaneously**, with "metric transplant" and "attention starvation" more prominent than the official story allows. |---|---|

Rather than a list of ideas, a map of *territories*, ordered from nearest to furthest. Distance correlates with both risk and diversification value, which is the whole tension.

**Ring 0 — Value capture inside the core.** Pricing architecture, packaging and tiering, attach rates, contract length, churn recovery, price realisation in under-monetised segments. Not diversification at all. But it is typically the cheapest earnings growth available to a mature niche leader, it requires no new capability, and — the point — **it can fund the entire diversification programme without touching reserves.** I'd want this run as a parallel workstream from month one by the flagship's own team, with its incremental contribution explicitly earmarked as the programme's funding source. It also buys political cover: a programme funded from found money is much harder to resent.

**Ring 1 — Attach around the flagship.** Consumables, service contracts, extended support tiers, training and certification, financing, implementation and managed services, compliance-as-a-service. Same buyer, same budget, same sales motion. Low diversification value in the fragility sense (correlated with the core), real value in growth and switching cost. Cheap. Do the good ones regardless of what else we decide.

**Ring 2 — Data and insight products from the installed base.** Benchmarking, industry indices, predictive maintenance, regulatory reporting. Uses an asset only we hold. Margin profile usually excellent. Two hard gates: contractual right to use the data, and whether customers will pay for insight they believe they already own. Requires genuine consent-based commercial design, not a legal loophole.

**Ring 3 — Adjacent steps in the buyer's workflow.** What our customer does immediately before and immediately after they use the flagship, and who they currently buy that from. This is, in my view, **the highest-expected-value territory** and where I'd want the most theses. Same buyer, same trust, same procurement path — but a genuinely new offering, new competitors, and often a new demand driver. The interesting question is never "what could we build?" but "which of our customer's adjacent problems is being served badly by someone who doesn't understand the domain?"

**Ring 4 — Same offering, adjacent buyers.** New verticals, new geographies, new segment tiers (a stripped-down offer for the mid-market we currently ignore; a sovereign or regulated variant). Reuses the product; requires new demand-side assets, which is exactly what we can't transfer. Cheaper than it looks on the supply side, more expensive than it looks on the demand side.

**Ring 5 — Capability transplant.** Our technical competence applied to a different customer base entirely. This is almost certainly the territory of at least one previous failure. Not forbidden — but it should be funded and governed as **venture**, at venture-sized cheques, and never as "an extension of the business."

**Ring 6 — Unrelated diversification.** Buying earnings streams for the sake of decorrelation. The board's instinct will drift here, and I'd rather say plainly now that it's a poor use of an operating company's balance sheet. Shareholders can diversify more cheaply than we can. **If the answer to fragility is financial, the right instruments are capital return, contract structure, insurance and balance-sheet strength — not conglomeration.**

Minimal capital, uses the installed-base asset directly, and produces a live map of which adjacencies customers actually want. It doubles as the cheapest market-research instrument available to us.

# Diversification Strategy — First Consultation Draft

*How this document is meant to be read.* This is a first draft written to be argued with, not approved. The numbers are **placeholders left deliberately visible so Finance and Corp Dev can correct them**; they describe a shape, not a position I'm attached to. Several sections are framed as questions rather than recommendations — not out of vagueness, but because a few of them genuinely cannot be settled from where I sit, and pretending otherwise would waste the room's time.

One process request. I'd rather this circulate to Finance, the flagship's business lead, whoever was closest to the two prior attempts (including the people who have since left, if they'll talk to us), and one or two long-standing customers' technical buyers, **before** it reaches the board. By the time it's discussed formally, nothing in it should be new to anyone in the room, and no one should be put in the position of having to disagree in public.

There are **three real decisions** in what follows. Everything else can proceed quietly in parallel and be adjusted.

---

## 1. What we are actually solving for

The board has named the problem as *concentration risk*. I'd like to gently widen that, because the framing determines which answers are even visible.

Ninety-five percent of revenue in one product is a fact, not yet a risk. It becomes a risk in the presence of a **discontinuity** — technology substitution, a channel or platform shift, buyer consolidation, regulatory change, a well-funded entrant willing to lose money for five years. A mature market growing at under 2% is not, by itself, dangerous. It is *dull*, and dullness is a different problem with different remedies.

So there are two distinct concerns tangled together, and it's worth pulling them apart before spending anything:

| Concern | What it actually is | What answers it |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | One shock removes most of our earnings | Reduce correlation of earnings sources; strengthen contracts, channels, balance sheet |
| **Stagnation** | Earnings are safe but will not grow | New demand — which may or may not mean new products |

These pull in different directions. An adjacency that grows nicely but fails in exactly the same scenario the flagship fails in solves stagnation and *nothing* about fragility. I'd propose we make that explicit and test for it (§5, correlation test), because it's the failure mode nobody catches until the shock arrives.

**Three framing observations I'd offer for the room to accept or reject:**

- **The honest baseline is not diversification. It is harvest-and-return.** A profitable niche leader in a slow market, run for cash and capital return, is a perfectly respectable outcome that beats most diversification attempts on a risk-adjusted basis. Unless "do nothing new, return the cash" is a genuinely available answer at every gate, the process becomes theatre and every proposal passes.
- **Our scarce resource is not cash. It is management attention and internal credibility.** Strong reserves are why the previous two attempts were *possible*; they were not sufficient. Cash lets you buy a bad idea faster.
- **Two failures have created an organisational allergy.** Whatever we do next will be watched by people who expect it to fail, some of whom would prefer to be right. That is a design constraint on governance (§8), not a morale problem to be jollied along.

---

## 2. Gate 0 (Months 0–3): the failure autopsy, and the capability audit

These two pieces of work are cheap, fast, and worth more than any market study we could commission. They are the first gate because everything downstream is shaped by what they find.

### 2.1 The autopsy

"They strayed too far from our capabilities" is the received explanation. It may well be right. I'd like to hold it loosely for a few weeks, because it is also a *comfortable* explanation — it locates the fault in the idea rather than in how we ran it, and it conveniently implies the remedy is simply "stay closer to home."

Method, and it should be done by someone with no stake in the answer:

1. Retrieve the original investment memos and board papers. Extract the **stated assumptions** — market size, time to revenue, who would sell it, what margin was promised.
2. Interview everyone who was materially involved, including the departed. Separately, not in a group.
3. Reconstruct the sequence of the actual failure: what broke first, and what the organisation did in response.
4. Classify against a taxonomy, because the remedies are entirely different:

| Failure mode | Signature | Remedy implied |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrong adjacency** | Genuinely no reusable asset; we were a random entrant | Better selection screen (§5) |
| **No distribution advantage** | Good product, our channel wouldn't or couldn't sell it | Channel test before build; separate go-to-market |
| **Metric transplant** | Judged on flagship margins/payback from year one; starved when it looked worse | Different metrics and funding rules (§8) |
| **Attention starvation** | Sponsor's day job reclaimed them; the venture became a side project | Dedicated leadership, protected time, named substitute |
| **Talent adverse selection** | Staffed with whoever was available, not who was best | Career-safe secondments, deliberate staffing |
| **One big bet** | Fully funded up front, no kill points, sunk-cost escalation | Stage gating (§7) |
| **Integration crush** | Acquisition's operating model dissolved into ours | Ring-fence, explicit integration doctrine |
| **Right idea, wrong decade** | Thesis validated later by someone else | Option retention rather than exit |

I'd expect us to find **two or three of these simultaneously**, with "metric transplant" and "attention starvation" more prominent than the official story allows. If so, the implication is uncomfortable but useful: our selection problem may be smaller than our *operating model* problem, and a better screen alone would not have saved either attempt.

**Deliverable:** a two-page classification, circulated to the people interviewed for correction before it goes anywhere else.

### 2.2 The capability audit — what we own that is actually portable

Every company believes it has transferable capabilities. Most of what gets listed is either not rare, not portable, or already fully monetised. The test I'd propose, applied asset by asset:

For each candidate asset, four questions: **Is it rare? Is it hard to copy? Is it portable outside the flagship's context? Is there value left in it that we are not currently capturing?** An asset must pass all four to count.

Likely candidates for a company in our position, with the honest verdict noted:

| Candidate asset | Usual reality |
|---|---|
| **Access to and trust with a specific buyer** | Often the single most valuable and most under-used asset. Demand-side. Portable across *offerings*, not across *buyers* |
| **Deep domain and regulatory knowledge** | Genuinely rare. Portable only within the domain |
| **Installed-base data / operational telemetry** | Frequently valuable, frequently unexamined, occasionally contractually unusable — check before building a thesis on it |
| **Certifications, approvals, audit history** | Rare, expensive to replicate, a real moat where they apply |
| **Support / field / service infrastructure** | Portable, and often has spare capacity |
| **Brand** | Portable *only within the permission the brand carries*. Test it (§5), don't assume it |
| **Engineering or manufacturing competence** | Usually less rare than we believe |
| **Cash** | Not a capability. Please let's not treat it as one |

**The screen I'd propose, and this is the one substantive rule I'd like to hold firm on:** a candidate adjacency must reuse **at least two** audited assets, and **at least one must be demand-side** — customer access, trust, brand permission, channel. Supply-side reuse alone ("we're good at building this sort of thing") produces competent products that nobody has any particular reason to buy from us. My working suspicion is that this is what happened at least once before.

---

## 3. Where to look: an adjacency map, ordered by distance

Rather than a list of ideas, a map of *territories*, ordered from nearest to furthest. Distance correlates with both risk and diversification value, which is the whole tension.

**Ring 0 — Value capture inside the core.** Pricing architecture, packaging and tiering, attach rates, contract length, churn recovery, price realisation in under-monetised segments. Not diversification at all. But it is typically the cheapest earnings growth available to a mature niche leader, it requires no new capability, and — the point — **it can fund the entire diversification programme without touching reserves.** I'd want this run as a parallel workstream from month one by the flagship's own team, with its incremental contribution explicitly earmarked as the programme's funding source. It also buys political cover: a programme funded from found money is much harder to resent.

**Ring 1 — Attach around the flagship.** Consumables, service contracts, extended support tiers, training and certification, financing, implementation and managed services, compliance-as-a-service. Same buyer, same budget, same sales motion. Low diversification value in the fragility sense (correlated with the core), real value in growth and switching cost. Cheap. Do the good ones regardless of what else we decide.

**Ring 2 — Data and insight products from the installed base.** Benchmarking, industry indices, predictive maintenance, regulatory reporting. Uses an asset only we hold. Margin profile usually excellent. Two hard gates: contractual right to use the data, and whether customers will pay for insight they believe they already own. Requires genuine consent-based commercial design, not a legal loophole.

**Ring 3 — Adjacent steps in the buyer's workflow.** What our customer does immediately before and immediately after they use the flagship, and who they currently buy that from. This is, in my view, **the highest-expected-value territory** and where I'd want the most theses. Same buyer, same trust, same procurement path — but a genuinely new offering, new competitors, and often a new demand driver. The interesting question is never "what could we build?" but "which of our customer's adjacent problems is being served badly by someone who doesn't understand the domain?"

**Ring 4 — Same offering, adjacent buyers.** New verticals, new geographies, new segment tiers (a stripped-down offer for the mid-market we currently ignore; a sovereign or regulated variant). Reuses the product; requires new demand-side assets, which is exactly what we can't transfer. Cheaper than it looks on the supply side, more expensive than it looks on the demand side.

**Ring 5 — Capability transplant.** Our technical competence applied to a different customer base entirely. This is almost certainly the territory of at least one previous failure. Not forbidden — but it should be funded and governed as **venture**, at venture-sized cheques, and never as "an extension of the business."

**Ring 6 — Unrelated diversification.** Buying earnings streams for the sake of decorrelation. The board's instinct will drift here, and I'd rather say plainly now that it's a poor use of an operating company's balance sheet. Shareholders can diversify more cheaply than we can. **If the answer to fragility is financial, the right instruments are capital return, contract structure, insurance and balance-sheet strength — not conglomeration.**

**One structural option worth its own line:** open the installed base as a **platform** — let third parties build, certify and sell into our customers, and take a share plus certification revenue. Minimal capital, uses the installed-base asset directly, and produces a live map of which adjacencies customers actually want. It doubles as the cheapest market-research instrument available to us.

---

## 4. Ring 0 caveat: protecting the core comes first

Before any of this, a commitment I'd like written into the programme charter rather than assumed:

- **The flagship's own investment plan is funded in full, first, at pre-programme levels or better.** The fastest way to endanger the core is to quietly tax it.
- **No more than [10]% of named key flagship personnel** may be reassigned to programme work, with the flagship's business lead holding a veto — not an advisory voice, a veto.
- **No customer becomes an unwilling pilot.** Every pilot is opt-in, with a named relationship owner who can stop it, and a written commitment about what happens if it's cancelled.
- **No cross-subsidy in pricing.** Bundling a venture into flagship contracts to manufacture adoption produces revenue that teaches us nothing and hides failure.
- **A cash floor** below which the programme pauses automatically, set by Finance and stated publicly, so that nobody has to be the person who raises it in a bad quarter.

---

## 5. How to evaluate candidates

A scorecard, so the argument happens once and nobody has to lose it repeatedly in meetings. Weights are placeholders; Finance and the flagship lead should set them.

| Criterion | Weight | What good looks like | Kill threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Demand-side asset reuse** | 25 | Same buyer, our name is an advantage | No demand-side reuse → kill |
| **Supply-side asset reuse** | 15 | Two or more audited assets | Fewer than one → kill |
| **Sales-motion compatibility** | 15 | Existing channel can sell it without changing comp | Needs a wholly new channel → reclassify as venture, re-price |
| **Correlation with core demand** | 15 | Fails in a *different* scenario than the flagship | Perfectly correlated → still fundable as growth, but scores zero

|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | One shock removes most of our earnings | Earnings sources that fail in *different* scenarios; contract structure; balance-sheet strength; capital return |
| **Stagnation** | Earnings are safe but will not grow | New demand — which may or may not require new products |

An adjacency sold to the same buyer through the same channel grows earnings and does almost nothing for fragility, because it dies in the same event. Most "diversification" programmes are anti-stagnation programmes wearing the other name. We should label ours honestly and budget for both (§6).

### 1.1 The concentration is worse than stated

| | Revenue | Contribution (illustrative) | Share of contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship | £190m | £85.5m @ 45% | **97.7%** |
| Everything else | £10m | £2.0m @ 20% | 2.3% |
| **Total** | **£200m** | **£87.5m** | |

A mature, defended niche product carries high margin precisely because the market is slow and the investment cycle is over. Everything we add — services, managed offerings, implementation, mid-market variants — will carry **lower gross margin and higher cost-to-serve**. So revenue concentration will fall faster than contribution concentration, and the board's real concern is earnings.

Two consequences we should agree now rather than discover in year two:

- **The target must be stated in contribution terms.** Revenue diversification is the easier number and the less meaningful one.
- **The programme is margin-dilutive for approximately four years, by design.** If new lines are judged against 45% flagship contribution in year two, they will be starved — which is one of the failure modes we are trying not to repeat.

### 1.2 Three framing points I will defend

- **Harvest-and-return is a live baseline at every gate.** A profitable niche leader run for cash and capital return beats most diversification attempts on a risk-adjusted basis. Unless "do nothing new, return the capital" is genuinely available at each gate, the gates are ceremonial and every proposal passes.
- **The scarce resource is management attention and internal credibility, not cash.** Cash was why the last two attempts were possible; it was not why they were sufficient. (Amending the first draft's line: cash is not a *substitute* for a capability. In a fragmented adjacency full of undercapitalised specialists, balance-sheet strength genuinely *is* a durable advantage — that is the core of a roll-up thesis, and §8 relies on it.)
- **Two visible failures have created an internal allergy.** People will watch this expecting it to fail. That is a governance design constraint, not a morale issue, and it is why §9 and §11 are as detailed as they are.
